## Abstract

We find that the initial, solvent-cast state of nanoparticles (NPs) in a polymer matrix temporally

evolves during thermal annealing such that, at steady state, NPs maximize their distance from each

other subject to mass balance constraints. The observed timescales for this unexpected structural

reorganization, as probed by small angle x-ray scattering, are temperature dependent and can be

prohibitively large, especially at temperatures around and below 1.2Tg. X-Ray Photon Correlation

Spectroscopy measurements during reorganization reveal that the collective NP dynamics slow

down with annealing at constant temperature; this is accompanied by changes in the low frequency

regime in macroscopic viscoelastic measurements in equilibrated materials. By ruling out other

potential sources for these effects (i.e., electrostatic interactions, adsorbed layers), we attribute

these results to a long-ranged repulsive force between the NPs caused by fluctuations in the

polymer phase, i.e. the “Anti-Casimir” effect proposed by Obhukhov and Semenov.1 Thus, our

results highlight the important role of long-term, slow NP reorganization on the structure and

subsequently the properties of PNCs, even in the case of nominally miscible polymer nanoparticle

hybrids.

## Introduction

Composite materials comprised of nanoparticles (NPs) added to a polymer matrix, termed as

polymer nanocomposites (PNCs), have been intensely studied over the past few decades. These

hybrids can have significantly altered properties relative to the host matrix,2-5 where changes in

mechanical,6-14 thermal,15-18 rheological,19-24 optical,25-28 transport,29-34 and electrical35-37

properties have been observed. While the presence of NPs often improve properties, dramatic

improvements are usually only observed when the fillers are uniformly dispersed in the matrix;

this is likely because the interfacial area allowing for interactions between the polymer and the

NPs is significantly increased with well dispersed NPs relative to their agglomerated analogs. The

generally accepted guiding principle for fabricating PNCs with dispersed nanoparticles is to utilize

polymers with functional groups which mediate the unfavorable interactions between the

(normally) hydrophilic NP and the (usually) hydrophobic polymer. The presence of these

interacting groups lead to the formation of a “bound layer”, comprised of polymer chains

physically adsorbed to the NP surface.38-40 This layer, which prevents NP agglomeration through

the steric stabilization mechanism (where the bound layer screens attractive van der Waals forces

between NPs leading to NP-NP contact), plays an important role in determining PNC rheological

and mechanical reponses,13, 41, 42 e.g., as discussed by Ondreas et al.43 and Zhao et al.6 At high NP

volume fractions, the bound layers on adjacent NPs could connect, leading to the formation of a

bridged network structure with a solid-like mechanical response.13, 44, 45 The idea of steric

stabilization also carries over to PNCs containing polymer-grafted nanoparticles (where polymer

chains tethered to the surface of the NP mediate unfavorable interactions between the matrix and

the NP) where, again, both the dispersion state and formation of a network structure affect the

mechanical and rheological properties.13, 19, 46, 47

Hooper and Schweizer studied the equilibrium structure of PNCs as a function of NP volume

fraction and interaction strengths between the polymer and the NP and provided design rules for

NP dispersion in polymers.48, 49 While attaining the equilibrium NP dispersion state is the ultimate

goal, many recent studies have highlighted how different processing conditions lead to different

PNC structures (and hence, potentially, favorable properties). These conditions include choice of

common solvent50-53 and evaporation rates,54, 55 external fields,56-58 and thermal annealing

conditions.59-61 It has been well established that polymer melts also exhibit differences in

properties based on the processing pathway used62, and thus the fact that most initial PNC states

are non-equilibrium, with an initial dispersion state that is highly dependent on the particular

processing pathway and any subsequent annealing is not surprising. Previously, Chen et al. found

that the viscosity of NP filled polystyrene increases with time and only approaches a steady state

after ~100 hours, much longer than chain reptation and bare NP diffusion times.63 They attributed

this to hindered mobility of the chains adsorbed on the surfaces of the NP, a phenomenon which

has attracted recent attention. Jimenez et al.64 and Bailey et al.65 found that the desorption and

exchange of adsorbed chains with the bulk surrounding polymer is dependent on temperature, with

measurable exchange only occurring when the temperature is high enough to activate the

desorption of multiple surface contacts of a chain. On the other hand, Mackay et al., in an attempt

to disperse NPs in a matrix with unfavorable NP-polymer interactions, found that rapid

precipitation provided a secondary protocol for obtaining well dispersed PNCs.66 However, Cabral

and coworkers found that these composites were also temporally unstable as in-situ SANS

experiments showed particle agglomeration over time.67 Thus, even PNCs with well dispersed NPs

evolve over longer than expected timescales.

In this work, we focus on thermal annealing and how it affects the temporal evolution of the

structure, dynamics and properties of model PNCs with nominally well dispersed SiO2 NPs.

Generally, thermally annealing removes residual casting solvent which might be present after

ambient drying. Secondly, heating the composite above the polymer’s glass transition temperature

(Tg; usually >1.2Tg ) allows it to equilibrate. Through in-situ SAXS experiments at fixed

temperature, we find that dispersion state of the NPs evolves from a random dispersion to more

correlated structures at timescales which are much longer than the corresponding relaxation times

of the polymer host. The structural evolution is accompanied by a slowdown in the relaxation time

of the NPs as measured through XPCS, indicating that the effective mobility of the NPs in the

matrix slows down significantly on the formation of the ordered state. This effect propagates in

the rheological response as there is significant low frequency reinforcement in the PNCs for the

composite with increasing NP weight fraction, which can be attributed to the formation of a

percolated structure with interacting bound layers. We propose that the evolution of the NP

structure is a consequence of the drying process where the NPs are kinetically arrested due to

increasing viscosity of the polymer phase. In the melt state, repulsive forces due to matrix

fluctuations result in the rearrangement of the NPs into more ordered arrangements with their

spacing being dictated by the volume fraction of the NPs. Thus, utilizing thermal energy to drive

the PNCs to equilibrium results in more ordered structures with slower NP dynamics and better

viscoelastic response.

## 2. Results and Discussion

All the systems we consider in this work are prototypical PNCs where steric stabilization of the

nanoparticles is achieved by a bound layer of polymer on the NP surface. If we consider the case

of P2VP, the strong hydrogen bond that can form between the nitrogen atom on the pyridine ring

and the hydrophilic silica surface is the driving force behind the formation of the bound layer.

Similar hydrogen bonding interactions also stabilize SiO2 NPs in PMA and PEO leading to steric

stabilization of the NPs, preventing irreversible aggregation. As shown in Figure 1A-1C, TEM

confirms the absence of visible aggregation of the 14 nm silica nanoparticles in the three different

polymers used in the study, P2VP, PMA and PEO, reinforcing the notion that nanoparticles are

nominally well dispersed in these composites. This is true for the larger NPs as well. (See

Supplementary Information, Figure S1). Note that the thicker PEO and PMA films from cryo-

microtoming have a large number of visible NPs despite the lower PNC concentrations (Slices are

100-200 nm compared to particle size of 14 nm).

2.1 Dispersion and Structural Evidence for Aging

Even though the composites are well dispersed when cast from solution, there are significant

discrepancies between the colloidal dispersion in the “as cast” materials compared to the materials

after annealing, though this is difficult to discern from TEM alone due to the thickness of the slice

and fewer number of particles observed in one image. SAXS reveals that the particles are nearly

uniformly dispersed in the as cast state (dark blue curve at t=0, Figure 2A,Figure S3) for 14 nm

SiO2 NPs in PMA with no indication of any large scale aggregation at low q. Regardless, after

annealing at temperatures well above the glass transition temperature of PMA (Tg ≈ 15 oC, Tanneal

= 120 oC), a significantly larger structure factor peak appears progressively with increasing time,

indicating that the particles have become more regularly spaced upon annealing. This is true for

NPs dispersed in PEO as well (see Supporting Information, Figure S4), with three different NP

sizes showing a structure factor peak after annealing at 120 oC for ~6 hours. Thus, this suggests

that there is significant NP mobility as they temporally rearrange in the PNCs, and the initial as

cast state is nowhere near its equilibrium configuration. We will return to this observation later in

this work.

timescale of the NPs (even though the motion by itself is not that of a freely diffusing particle).

The origins of compressed exponential behavior for the dynamics of NPs dispersed in a polymer

matrix has been a topic of continued discussion. For colloidal gels, Bouchaud and Pitard91

proposed that microscopic stress relaxations lead to the ballistic behavior. The accumulation of

microcollapses leads to an increase in relaxation time with aging time. Cipeletti et al. found that

even jammed colloidal systems display the compressed exponential behavior and could be

attributed to the internal stresses.92 Srivastava et al. also modified the theory for applications in

polymer nanocomposites.84 The systems considered in this work are all probed at temperatures

above 1.2Tg, which means that dynamical heterogeneities caused by the glassy nature of the

polymer and their associated stress relaxations likely do not contribute to the behavior observed.

Bridging associated network formation can lead to a glass/gel like viscoelastic response,19, 93 yet

as we noted previously, the mean NP-NP spacing for the lower NP weight fraction as well as the

larger 50 nm particles is larger than the expected interaction distance of NP-NP polymer bridges

thus making such an explanation unlikely. Jimenez et al.64 and Bailey et al.65 have previously

shown that the bound polymer layer is dynamic and polymer chains do exchange with the

surrounding bulk polymer and, thus, the fluctuations associated with this effect might lead to a

localized stress field, leading to the compressed relaxations observed here.

The correlation between slow (local) nanoparticle motion and mechanical reinforcement has been

noted before by Senses et al. for PEO based composites with different weight fractions of SiO2

NPs.78 Similarly, Akcora et al. reported that the gel-like reinforcement in composites with grafted

nanoparticles was accompanied by a marked decrease in the NP mobility.79 There was a significant

degree of dynamical aging observed in that study as well, but one that was attributed to the

formation of anisotropic structures with time for the GNP/matrix combination used.60 To test the

## 3. Discussion

The previous sections highlighted the non-equilibrium nature of the NP dispersion in a polymer

matrix and how extensive thermal annealing leads to changes in the nanoscale NP organization.

This affects the NP mobility in the matrix as well as the PNC macroscopic properties.

Theoretically, the reorganization of NPs into short-ranged correlated structures would be an

entropically unfavorable process as the configurational entropy of a random dispersion of NPs

would be higher than that of a uniform dispersion of NPs.97 Thus, we believe that a secondary

long-ranged repulsive potential must exist which drives the NPs into their final equilibrium

structures. For block copolymers adsorbed on flat surfaces, Tirrell and coworkers have previously

measured a repulsive force at distances much larger than the coil size of the unadsorbed block (up

to 4Rg),  which is in line with our assumption of a long ranged repulsive potential.98 Qualitatively,

this repulsive potential explains the long range ordering of the NPs as well as the corresponding


<!-- Page 24 -->


24

decrease in mobility of the NPs. In the absence of any force which drives the NPs to obey mass

balance constraints, steric stabilization and bridging between NPs due to bound polymer chains

would be the expected phase behavior, as has been predicted by Hooper and Schweizer.49 Such a

model has been quantitatively used to describe scattering patterns and real space structure in recent

work focused on P2VP/SiO2 PNCs.44 The bound layer preventing contact aggregation between the

NPs and act akin to a short-ranged repulsive potential, the range of which is dictated by the size of

the bound layer. Thus, as long as conditions promoting the formation of a bound layer remain, the

NPs will not be able to move to a state where NP aggregates are the favored state. As indicated

previously, the well accepted size of the bound polymer layer is based on the Rg of the polymer

chain (5.3 nm for 44 kDa), which is lower than the surface to surface spacing at for low weight

fractions (3-10 wt.%; 30, 20 nm) of 14 nm SiO2 NPs. This is also apparent for the dispersion of 50

nm NPs in PEO, as the NP surface to surface spacing for 14 wt.% NPs in PEO is 40 nm which is

again much larger than the Rg of 40 kDa PEO (5.3 nm). (Figure S17)

Thus, a simple argument based on steric stabilization from the bound polymer layer cannot explain

the observations of interparticle spacing at the lowest volume fractions and decreased ballistic

velocity observed through XPCS, the next most obvious origin of repulsive forces comes from the

charged double layer on the surface of the NPs which stabilize it in solution. Qiu et al.99, Meth et

al.100 and Poling-Skutvik et al.101 were able to model the structure of dispersed NPs in a polymer

solution by invoking the surface charge and utilizing the Hayter-Penfold Rescaled Mean Spherical

Approximation (HPRMSA)102 to fit the equilibrium SAXS curves. However, Meth et al.100 observe

the apparent collapse of the charged double layer during the process of drying, with the appearance

of a scattering pattern similar to what is observed for aggregated nanoparticles as more of the


<!-- Page 25 -->


25

solvent evaporates. Such an observation was also made by us in our studies (see for example,

Figure S9), but annealing at elevated temperatures reverses this phenomenon with time. While

electrostatic repulsion seems like a plausible explanation for the development of the resulting NP

structure, recent experiments in our group have shown that this aging phenomenon occurs in

PEO/NP mixtures with added salt, even in cases where the Debye length is on the order of a few

Angstroms. As the debye length governs the range of interaction, this surface charge induced effect

also seems unlikely to be relevant in this context.51, 53

In the absence of any other argument, the only other explanation which is able to explain most of

the other observations comes from work by Obukhov and Semenov.1 They predicted that

fluctuations in the polymer phase would result in a long ranged (longer than a few monomers)

repulsive force (termed as the anti-Casimir effect) between objects in a polymer melt. In the limit

of long chains, these forces scale as a (n = -3) power law of the ratio of the NP size to the NP

separation (for infinitely long chains) and can thus be operative even at distances of 54 nm, which

is the mean spacing between 14nm NPs at a 3 wt.% in PMA.  At the simplest level, the repulsive

force can explain the observation of NPs following the contraints of mass balance, as well as the

reduction in XPCS derived ballistic velocity, as the motion will be based on a force balance on a

particle. As the magnitude of the force is likely dependent on the chain length, we expect changes

in the degree of correlation with changing molecular weight of the matrix. This is indeed observed,

as the hard-sphere volume fraction of the SAXS fits changes from 0.02 for a molecular weight of

23 kDa to 0.20 for 4 wt.% 14 nm NPs in 96 kDa PMA (Figure S15). This further lends credence

to a chain size fluctuation mediated repulsive force which determines structure, dynamics and

properties in equilibrated PNCs. An important note here is that the formalism for the anti-Casimir

force is based on non-interacting spherical inclusions in a polymer matrix. It is not well understood

how the bound polymer layer would influence the manifestation of the force, and remains an open

question.

## 4. Conclusions

We show that NPs well dispersed in a polymer matrix during solvent casting evolve significantly

over time until they reach an equilibrium associated with the loading of the NPs, and the polymer

molecular weight. The timescales for structural reorganization at temperatures around 1.2Tg can

take weeks to reach its final form for 14nm SiO2 NPs dispersed in PMA, making these timescales

prohibitively large, in a system with relatively low Tg and MW. For systems with less mobility

(e.g. P2VP, PS), an equilibrium is likely to never be reached at all, leaving PNCs to be annealed

to arbitrarily rearranged states. The structural reorganization is also accompanied by a concomitant

slowing down in the dynamics of the NPs in the matrix, as seen through X-Ray Photon Correlation

Spectroscopy (XPCS) as well as on the macroscopic viscoelastic response. After extensive

annealing of the PNCs, significant low frequency reinforcement is observed for the composites

and a steady state zero-shear viscosity cannot be achieved within the frequency windows studied.

The changes in low frequency reinforcement is dependent on the NP loading, as samples with low

loadings of NPs still show liquid-like viscoelastic response but with a significantly increased

viscosity. We attribute the structural reorganization to a repulsive force between the NPs due to

fluctuations in the polymer phase. This highlights the important role thermal annealing plays in

determining macroscopic properties, and it also provides insight into the difficulty in comparing

data from similarly fabricated materials which are treated in different manners, as a “true

equilibrium” might not have been reached.

Thermal Properties

Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC)

A TA Instruments Discovery DSC was used for thermal property measurements. The instrument

was calibrated with a sapphire disk for heat capacity and indium for temperature and enthalpy.

Fragments of a disk (~10 mg) were loaded in to aluminum pans and accurate weight measures

were obtained with the TGA. Annealed samples loaded in to the aluminum pans were run under a

nitrogen environment with a ramp rate of 2 oC /min and a temperature modulation of 1.27 oC for

60 seconds while cooling from 80 oC to -20 oC. Prior to the cooling step, the pans were equilibrated

at 80 oC for 1 hour. Glass transition temperatures estimated from the first derivative of the

reversing heat capacity (Cp,rev) and are reported in the Supporting Information.

Thermogravimetric analysis

A TA Instruments thermogravimetric analyzer was used to measure the final weight fraction of

SiO2 NPs in the composites. The instrument was calibrated with Nickel and Alumel for Curie point

temperature calibrations and standardized weights provided by TA Instruments. 5-10 mg of sample

were loaded on to a platinum pan and heated to 700 oC under O2 flow with a ramp rate of 10

oC/min. Terminal steady state was achieved well before the 700 oC limit and the final mass

obtained was used to estimate final NP loadings in the PNCs.

Small angle x-ray scattering (SAXS) was performed on a laboratory system at Columbia

University (Ganesha, SAXSLAB) with a Cu KB source (λ = 1.54 Å), a spot size of ~200x200 µm,

Ultra UCT Microtome at -80 oC. P2VP samples were microtomed at room temperature on the same

measurement. Two-time correlation functions were calculated to ensure that we are sampling

homogenous dynamics across one intensity autocorrelation function and not heterogenous

dynamics which are changing over the measurement time. Calculation details and a representative
